source.title: Towards Multimodal Interpretability: Learning Sparse Interpretable Features in Vision Transformers

record.file_problem: none; full post and comments are present
record.tranche_reason: Reports SAE reconstruction and downstream-loss results in a CLIP vision transformer setting, bearing on the loss consequence named in V3. It does not test the other dark-matter claims.
record.gate_note: The post reports SAE reconstruction metrics and evaluates CLIP loss with the SAE inserted. It does not measure linear predictability of SAE error, per-token error scaling or overlap across SAE sizes, compare reconstruction errors with equal-sized random errors, separate linear from nonlinear error, or test circuits or steering. Feature examples, sparsity, cluster, and neuron-alignment analyses do not test these claim versions.
record.test_reason: The study inserts an SAE into CLIP ViT-L (layer 22 class token) and compares contrastive loss with the original model on ImageNet-1k. This bears on the loss-harm part of V3 in a new vision/multimodal setting. No other version is tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The author's main conclusion is that SAEs find sparse, highly interpretable features in a CLIP ViT, with no dead features and L0 of 26. The lower loss with the SAE is called unexplained. In comments, the author tentatively attributes it to the ImageNet evaluation distribution: added error may separate tightly clustered fine-grained class representations, such as dog breeds. Explained variance was only 86%.
record.recipe_differences: The post trains an SAE on the class-token residual stream of a CLIP vision transformer and evaluates contrastive loss; it does not analyze dark-matter error predictability or compare reconstruction errors with random errors.
record.problems: For the V3-relevant result, there is no equal-sized random-error comparison or reported uncertainty. The author says the lower loss is not understood. The reported evaluation is on ImageNet-1k, with text prompts using the ImageNet labels.
record.rows_left_out: Feature examples and visualisations, sparsity statistics, ultra-low-density cluster analyses, and neuron-alignment results were left out because they do not measure any version's stated prediction about SAE error or its functional consequences. The random-vector comparison in the neuron-alignment section concerns neuron alignment, not random errors of the same size as SAE reconstruction error.

untested.parts: All: no linear prediction of SAE error from activations.
All: one SAE evaluated for loss; no per-token error norms or cross-size comparison (the expansion-16 SAE is only described via feature clusters).
Comparison of SAE-error loss impact against random errors of equal norm.
All: no circuits or steering analyses.
All: no comparison of training objectives or architectures on error size.

missing.what: Explained variance of the SAE reconstruction is 86% (author calls it lower than desired); a reconstruction-quality figure relevant context for r3
missing.locator: Training Performance — MSE, l1 and Model Losses

record.verdict_notes: Single informal LessWrong post with one SAE, no uncertainty, and no random-error control. The author's own hypothesis is that random error would also reduce loss on ImageNet. If so, the SAE's errors could still be worse than random, so the result should not be read as refuting V3's pathological-error claim. Hence limits_scope rather than challenges.

versions.untested_parts: Whether a large share of SAE error is a linear function of the input activation.
Per-token error-norm predictability across SAE sizes, whether larger SAEs fail on the same contexts, and whether error persists with scale.
The post does not compare SAE reconstruction errors with random errors of the same size.
Whether linear error contains unlearned features and nonlinear error is qualitatively different or resists further dictionary learning.
Whether circuits or steering analyses lose behavior when the SAE error term is omitted.
Whether SAE training choices cause dark matter or whether better architectures or end-to-end training reduce it.

conditions.value: output of layer 22 (of 24), residual stream of class token

rows.locator: Training Performance — MSE, l1 and Model Losses; author comment clarifying the loss evaluation
rows.note: The post states that the model with the SAE has lower loss than the original model. This runs opposite to the predicted loss harm, but the study does not compare against random errors of the same size.
rows.check: Loss with the SAE (1.775) is lower than the original (1.895), so reconstruction does not harm loss here. Two caveats apply. There is no equal-norm random-error baseline, so the pathological-vs-random comparison cannot be read. The evaluation is on ImageNet with label prompts, a distribution CLIP was not trained on, which the author suspects drives the drop.

relationships.condition: CLIP ViT-L layer-22 class-token SAE, contrastive loss evaluated on ImageNet-1k with 'A photo of a {label}.' prompts
relationships.reason: Splicing in the SAE lowers loss (1.775 vs 1.895, r3), so no loss harm appears in this out-of-distribution evaluation. Without a random-error baseline, the 'worse than random' core of V3 is neither confirmed nor refuted.
relationships.display_finding: Reconstruction substitution lowered contrastive loss from 1.895 to 1.775 in the out-of-distribution evaluation; no random-error comparison was reported.
